claims.text: Creep in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is governed by stress-induced short-range ordering at nanoscale interfaces.
Interface short-range ordering mediates dislocation activation and climb.
The starting multilayer has chemically disordered or weakly clustered FCC/BCC interfaces.
A temperature window exists in which diffusion-assisted dislocation processes are active while the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact.
Stress-driven atomic rearrangements at FCC/BCC interfaces produce localized regions with increased short-range order.
The resulting interface ordering alters dislocation mobility.
High-entropy alloys inherently exhibit compositional complexity and severe lattice distortion.
Under sustained load, lattice distortion and compositional complexity promote a transition from clustering or weak order to stronger order at multilayer interfaces.
Local interface ordering reduces the energy barrier for dislocation climb and glide.
The reduced barrier to dislocation motion progressively increases creep deformation.
The proposed ordering-assisted deformation retains the overall structural cohesion of the multilayer.
Relative to the starting material, sustained loading will cause a progressive increase in creep rate.
The creep-rate increase will be accompanied by detectable changes in interface chemistry and atomic ordering.
Dislocation structures will become spatially correlated with interface regions exhibiting short-range order.
The material will exhibit a time-dependent balance between strain hardening and softening.
The proposed mechanism requires retention of discrete nanoscale layers and may change after interlayer mixing or grain coarsening.
At temperatures too low for sufficient atomic mobility, stress-induced interface ordering will not occur.
At temperatures high enough to cause complete homogenization, the proposed interface-ordering mechanism will not operate.
Prior evidence shows that stress or high-strain deformation can induce short-range ordering in high-entropy alloys.
Failure to develop increased interface short-range order together with no significant creep-rate difference between initially disordered and pre-ordered samples would falsify the hypothesis.
